source_text: Post ista omnia in consummatione orationis uenit clausula uniuersas petitiones et preces nostras collecta breuitate concludens. in nouissimo enim ponimus: sed libera nos a malo, conprehendentes aduersa cuncta quae contra nos in hoc mundo molitur inimicus, a quibus potest esse firma et fida tutela, si nos Deus liberet, si deprecantibus adque inplorantibus opem suam praestet. quando autem dicimus libera nos a malo, nihil remanet quod ultra adhuc debeat postulari, quando semel protectionem Dei aduersus malum petamus, qua inpetrata contra omnia quae diabolus et mundus operantur securi stamus et tuti. quis enim uel de saeculo metus est cui in saeculo Deus tutor est?
thought_title: The final petition as complete protection
orientation: Cyprian is explaining the last petition of the Lord's Prayer, 'but deliver us from evil,' after having treated the earlier petitions.
pass_a_gloss: After all these things, at the completion of the prayer, comes a closing clause that concludes all our petitions and prayers with a gathered brevity. For in the last place we say: but deliver us from evil, comprehending all the adverse things that the enemy contrives against us in this world, from which there can be firm and faithful protection, if God delivers us, if he furnishes his help to those praying and imploring. But when we say deliver us from evil, nothing remains that ought still to be asked beyond this, when once we ask for the protection of God against evil, by which obtained we stand secure and safe against all things that the devil and the world work. For what fear is there even from the world for him for whom God is guardian in the world?

choices.why: Keeps the technical sense of a concluding formula that seals the prayer, not just a general 'ending.'
Preserves the image of all petitions being collected together into one brief statement.
Captures the active plotting sense of molior against us.
Keeps the alliteration and the double quality of the protection.
Preserves the paired adjectives and the standing posture of confidence.

pass_b_english: After all these things, at the end of the prayer comes a closing clause that gathers all our petitions and requests together in a brief conclusion. For at the very last we say: but deliver us from evil, taking in all the hostile things that the enemy contrives against us in this world. From which there can be firm and faithful protection if God delivers us, if he grants his help to us as we pray and implore him. When we say deliver us from evil, nothing remains that should still be asked for beyond this, once we ask for God's protection against evil. When that protection is obtained, we stand secure and safe against everything the devil and the world are working. For what fear of the world is there for someone whose guardian in the world is God?

problems.quote: From these there can be firm and faithful protection
problems.source_quote: a quibus potest esse firma et fida tutela
problems.why: English omits 'a quibus' ('from which'), breaking the causal link between the enemy's works and the need for protection.
problems.fix: from which there can be firm and faithful protection
problems.ruling: Source 'a quibus' links protection to preceding adversities; English 'From these' partially preserves it but loses the relative pronoun's grammatical connection.

edits.old: From these there can be firm and faithful protection
edits.new: From which there can be firm and faithful protection

fixed: Added 'a quibus' ('from which') to preserve the causal link between the enemy's works and the need for protection.

last_rejected.quote: For what fear of the world is there for someone whose guardian in the world is God?
last_rejected.source_quote: quis enim uel de saeculo metus est cui in saeculo Deus tutor est?
last_rejected.why: Source asks 'what fear even of the world' (uel = even), English drops intensifier.
last_rejected.fix: For what fear even of the world is there for one whose protector in the world is God?
last_rejected.ruling: 'uel' here is a rhetorical intensifier ('even'); dropping it is a minor omission, not a major meaning change.
